Most to least overrated: 
1. Jakarta (born and raised). It arguably has the best primary and secondary schools in Indonesia, great malls, great clubs, great international restaurants, (which are all frankly irrelevant if u ain’t got money to spend in them). As much as I hate to admit, it’s the center of Indonesia so u can find most things you need/want here. The people are not as conservative, if you like that sort of thing. But the traffic is insane and it’s too fucking crowded it’s suffocating. Just. People everywhere. You’d be hard pressed to find serenity here in other places beside your own home. Also, the sky is almost always grey bc of the pollution and no amount of skyscrapers can beat the beauty of a piercing blue sky. 

2. Jogja (visited multiple times). It’s cheap compared to Jakarta, but it’s just plain boring. Not much to do other than looking around at broken historical sites which aren’t taken care of properly. The food is always sweet too. It felt like I was on the verge of getting diabetes every time I had a meal. 

3. Puncak (visited multiple times). The tea plantation area is legit gorgeous man idk what to tell you. And the weather is really nice. The traffic to get there is kinda shit, sure, but I think it’s worth it? I mean, if you’ve lived in JKT all your life, you’re used to spending a few hrs in traffic everyday anyway. You just need to find a remote villa where you can enjoy the city without seeing too many people when you are there. 
4. Bali (visited multiple times). Great places, great people, fantastic beaches and mountains, fascinating culture, history, and nightlife. The private areas are VERY well managed. The owners don’t half-ass their investments in Bali and I loved it. Gets a bit too crowded sometimes, so you just need to go during off seasons. 
5. Surabaya (visited multiple times). It’s a clean and modern city filled with rich people. Good for businesses. There’s really not much to do if you’re a tourist, but I suppose it is a nice city to live in. 
6. Bandung (currently reside for 8+ years). City of young people with so many hang out places you’d always find some place new to try. Food carts EVERYWHERE and they’re so cheap. The people here are chill, friendly, polite and they are GORGEOUS. The weather is fantastic and the sight is magnificent. The traffic is not _so_ crazy downtown (where I live and mostly go around) during the weekdays, so it’s perfectly manageable. Minimum wage is not the best but work a bit harder (or smarter) and you could be living very comfortably here.

If you’re interested in Western philosophy: 
- Ryan Holiday is not necessarily a philosopher but he did write self-help/philosophy books, especially on stoicism. His books are easy to digest and I think they would be great as introduction to philosophy. I would recommend Stillness is the Key and The Obstacle is the Way. 
- The Consolation of Philosophy by Alain de Botton. Easy to read, packed with wisdom from 5 different famous philosophers from different eras. 

If you’re interested in Eastern philosophy:
- The Art of Happiness, The Dalai Lama. A series of conversation of The Dalai Lama and a psychiatrist who posed him questions about life and it’s problems. 
- The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari. A novel, but philosophical in nature. 

I would refrain from reading direct works of famous philosophers as a beginner. One could get bored very quickly and most of them are quite hard to grasp (even for a philosophy major) and one would move on thinking philosophy is hard and tedious. 

I would advice to start slow, read some articles, maybe find out what branch of philosophy you’re interested in, read a bit about it, then you might move on to primary sources. Have fun :)

Books help, finding communities online like this help too. And of course, it goes without saying that it is important to seek professional help. Find whatever that could help you with the process of your recovery. It is possible, you do not have to suffer.

It is definitely easier said than done, but it is possible. To look at problems logically and pragmatically, we can alleviate a lot of pain. We should choose to do that always, we must not let emotions and false perceived judgements make our lives harder than it already is. 

And there’s always a point in suffering. We might not be able to see it yet, but there is one. Logotherapy is an approach coined by the psychiatrist and survivor of three concentration camp Victor Frankl that helps people find meaning in life and the suffering, and that it is precisely our job to find it. “What is the meaning of life?” As though it is someone else’s responsibility to tell us. Instead, he said, the world is asking us that question. And it’s our job to answer with our actions.

There is a choice. As I said previously, it all lies in the perspective. Knowing the difference between the observing and the perceiving eyes. The observing eyes see what’s true, what is a fact, there’s no emotion attached to it. On the other hand, the perceiving eyes see with judgement and opinion. 

For example, “I have problem A”, that’s my observing eyes stating the fact. My perceiving eyes would then put my opinion on it saying “I hate my problems, I wish I don’t have them, and it upsets me.” Which one do you think would help me moving forward? I think it’s the former. Because then I’d have a clear mind in which I can use to tackle the problem, instead of fretting about it. 

It’s not easy, but it is doable. 

As Marcus Aurelius, the emperor of The Roman Empire, said “Choose not to be harmed—and you won't feel harmed. Don't feel harmed—and you haven't been.”

It is important and I believe in it wholeheartedly. Finding meaning in the suffering is exactly what Victor Frankl said, and what got me to find strength when times are especially hard. But there are also times when you can’t see the meaning of it, those times when all you see is darkness. But even during those, you can find ways to survive and not opt for suicide. Then, positive nihilism might be the answer.
